sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: The use of reversible fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR) inhibitors leads to the emergence of “undruggable” FGFR2 kinase domain mutations, hampering sequential treatment strategies. Lirafugratinib and futibatinib are irreversible FGFR inhibitors with the most promising clinical activity against FGFR2-driven tumors.

sec.title: Experimental Design:
sec.p: We characterized resistance to lirafugratinib with circulating tumor DNA, tissue whole-exome sequencing, and bulk RNA sequencing in 30 patients with FGFR2-driven cancers, treated in the phase I/II ReFocus trial (NCT04526106) and enrolled in the UNLOCK program at Gustave Roussy.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Among the 30 patients included, 18 (60%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 12 (40%) had other tumor types. Twenty-two patients (73%) were FGFR inhibitor–naïve. Among those experiencing primary resistance to lirafugratinib, we identified potential resistance mechanisms in five of six pretreatment samples. Patients with acquired lirafugratinib resistance manifested an unprecedented emergence of FGFR2 mutations in the M538 and/or L618 residues of the kinase domain, documented in 11 of 16 cases (69%). Compared with futibatinib resistance, FGFR2 molecular brake (N550) and gatekeeper (V565) mutations were rare. Leveraging the spectrum of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at resistance to lirafugratinib and futibatinib, respectively, we identified the complementarity of the two irreversible inhibitors. On the basis of viability assays in FGFR2::BICC1–dependent Ba/F3 models and in vivo studies on patient-derived xenografts, we propose treatment sequences with the two agents. After lirafugratinib progression, three patients received futibatinib and experienced prolonged disease response.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: The complementary activity of lirafugratinib and futibatinib against FGFR2 kinase domain mutations supports their sequential use when precise resistance mutations are detected in patients.

boxed-text.p: After the first generation of reversible fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR) inhibitors, the irreversible agents lirafugratinib and futibatinib are currently the FGFR inhibitors with the most promising clinical activity against FGFR2-driven tumors. We unveiled here the landscape of resistance to the selective FGFR2 inhibitor lirafugratinib and evaluated its complementarity with futibatinib against FGFR2 kinase domain mutations. In FGFR2::BICC1–dependent cellular Ba/F3 models, we validated the activity of futibatinib against mutations in FGFR2 M538 and L618 residues, whereas lirafugratinib overcame resistance mediated by mutations occurring in FGFR2 molecular brake (N550) and gatekeeper (V565) residues. We have previously showed the preclinical and clinical activity of a futibatinib–lirafugratinib sequence. In the present work, the possibility of a lirafugratinib–futibatinib one, suggested by the complementarity of the two inhibitors, was corroborated in patient-derived xenografts. After progressing on lirafugratinib, three patients received futibatinib with prolonged benefit, reinforcing the role of this sequence in clinical practice.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The identification of targetable molecular alterations of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) has opened a new era in the field of precision oncology. Currently, pemigatinib (reversible FGFR1–3 inhibitor) and futibatinib (irreversible FGFR1–4 inhibitor) are approved for the treatment of patients with advanced FGFR2-driven cholangiocarcinoma (1, 2). The prevalence of FGFR2 fusions in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (10%–15%) has indeed prompted the clinical development of selective inhibitors in this disease (3–5). Nevertheless, FGFR inhibitors have shown promising activity and efficacy across tumor types, in the presence of FGFR2 molecular driver alterations such as fusions, mutations, and amplifications (6–8).

Primary and acquired resistance mechanisms to selective FGFR inhibitors have been investigated in the setting of FGFR2-driven cholangiocarcinoma and other solid tumors. De novo resistance is less well characterized and likely attributable to off-target molecular events (9). On the other hand, the distinctive features of acquired resistance have been evident since the first reports, revealing the recurrent polyclonality of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations identified via circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) analysis (10–12). More recent works reported differential traits in the spectrum of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in patients progressing on reversible inhibitor (e.g., pemigatinib, infigratinib, and erdafitinib) versus the irreversible inhibitor futibatinib (9, 13). Resistance to reversible FGFR inhibitors arises from mutations throughout the FGFR2 kinase domain, with notable enrichment in the molecular brake (N550) and gatekeeper (V565) residues at progression on futibatinib. Off-target alterations in effectors of the MAPK and PI3K/mTOR pathways are recurrently found as well, mainly in concomitance to FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (9, 13, 14). Although MAPK pathway alterations may contribute significantly to resistance, the high frequency of PIK3CA mutations before exposure to FGFR inhibitors without any clear impact on clinical outcomes suggests their limited role in resistance (13, 15).

Lirafugratinib is an irreversible, FGFR2-selective inhibitor (16, 17). Its main and novel feature is represented by its activity against molecular brake and gatekeeper FGFR2 mutations. Moreover, its unique selectivity for FGFR2, sparing the other members of the FGFR family (FGFR1, 3, and 4), is aimed to provide a better therapeutic window for clinical use.

In the ReFocus trial (NCT04526106), FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients with FGFR2-driven solid tumors were treated at the recommended phase II dose (RP2D) of lirafugratinib (70 mg daily), with objective response rates (ORR) that ranged from 13% to 88%, and disease control rates (DCR) from 42% to 100% (18–20). The lowest activity was seen in diseases other than cholangiocarcinoma harboring an FGFR2 mutation, and the highest in patients with FGFR2-rearranged cholangiocarcinoma. Despite the low response rate in FGFR2-mutated cases, the duration of response ranged from 9.2 to more than 14.9 months, suggesting that prolonged benefit is still achievable in a molecularly selected subgroup of patients (20). In FGFR2-rearranged noncholangiocarcinoma tumors (n = 44), lirafugratinib achieved a confirmed ORR of 37%, with a median duration of response of 7.3 months (21). The activity of lirafugratinib was also evaluated in patients with FGFR2-rearranged cholangiocarcinoma who had progressed on a previous selective FGFR inhibitor (19). Among the 14 patients treated with lirafugratinib at 70 mg daily or higher, the ORR was 21%, DCR was 93%, 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 43%, and median duration of response was 5.6 months.

With these promising preliminary data across FGFR2 alterations and tumor types, lirafugratinib is expected to stay engaged in clinical practice. In this study, we were able to identify a distinctive pattern of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib by analyzing samples (ctDNA and tissue biopsies) from patients included in the ReFocus trial and assessed in the institutional UNLOCK program running at Gustave Roussy. FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients frequently developed a limited number of mutations, with a major enrichment at the M538 and L618 residues. Modeling these mutations in FGFR2::BICC1–driven cellular models, we confirmed that they conferred high levels of resistance to lirafugratinib, which low doses of futibatinib could overcome. We corroborated these findings by overcoming lirafugratinib resistance with futibatinib in patient-derived xenografts (PDX). Structural analyses revealed that the different binding interactions of the two inhibitors within the FGFR2 kinase domain represent the basis for their divergent activity against FGFR2 mutations. The sequential treatment strategy was also effective in three patients who experienced disease response to futibatinib after progression on lirafugratinib. By providing the molecular landscape of resistance to lirafugratinib supported by functional experiments and clinical evidence, we propose a novel treatment sequence with the two irreversible FGFR inhibitors.

sec.title: Patients and molecular analyses
sec.p: This study evaluated patients with advanced FGFR2-driven tumors included in the phase I/II ReFocus trial (NCT04526106) and treated with lirafugratinib at the RP2D of 70 mg daily. Post-progression molecular testing by targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) on ctDNA, with or without whole-exome sequencing (WES) and bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of tissue biopsy, was required for inclusion. In patients experiencing primary resistance to lirafugratinib, pretreatment molecular analyses were sufficient for inclusion.

As per common definition, patients with a best objective response (BOR) of progressive disease or a stable disease (SD) with a PFS (according to RECIST) less than 6 months were considered having primary resistance to lirafugratinib. A BOR of partial response of any duration or a SD with a PFS more than 6 months was consistent with acquired resistance (9, 22).

Molecular studies were performed in the setting of the UNLOCK program, an institutional program aiming to decipher mechanisms of action and resistance to innovative drugs. The cohort dedicated to lirafugratinib resistance is labeled UNLOCK-03. Furthermore, the majority of patients (26/30) were included in the institutional clinical molecular study STING (NCT04932525; patient identifiers starting with ST), and the remaining four in MATCH-R (NCT02517892; patient identifiers starting with MR; ref. 23).

All patients were fully informed and signed a written informed consent. The studies have been approved by ethics committees in France (French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety) and are being conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

ctDNA analyses were performed with Foundation Medicine, Illumina, or IntegraGen liquid biopsy panels. For the three panels, variant allele frequency (VAF) thresholds for calling mutations were <0.1%. Tissue biopsies underwent WES (mean coverage 140x) and bulk RNA-seq when the proportion of tumor cells ≥30%. Only molecular alterations potentially implicated in resistance were reported in the study. In line with publications from other groups, FGFR2 kinase domain mutations were reported according to reference transcript NM_001144913.1, according to which FGFR2 residues are, as an example, M538, N550, V565, and L618 (11, 15, 24). Of note, several articles used the reference transcript NM_000141.4, according to which the corresponding FGFR2 residues are M537, N549, V564, and L617 (10, 17).

As per common definition, the presence of >1 FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in a patient at a given time point defines those mutations as “polyclonal” (10), despite that their true clonality could not be assessed, and only in few cases their allelic status could be evaluated.

sec.title: Gene set enrichment analysis on RNA-seq data from tissue biopsies of FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients
sec.p: The available bulk RNA-seq data from tissue biopsies of FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients were analyzed. Differential gene expression between samples of patients experiencing primary versus acquired resistance or between acquired resistance samples harboring FGFR2 kinase domain mutations versus off-target alterations only was assessed using DESeq2 (Research Resource Identifier, RRID: SCR_000154) following variance stabilizing transformation normalization of count data. Hallmark gene sets were obtained from the MSigDB H collection. Genes were ranked according to the DESeq2 Wald test statistic, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA, RRID: SCR_003199) was performed using the GSEA function from the clusterProfiler package (RRID: SCR_016884). Hallmark pathways were considered significantly enriched if they met a false discovery rate–adjusted P value <0.01, using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and showed a normalized enrichment score ≥1.5 or ≤−1.5.

sec.title: Comparison of the spectrum of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at resistance to lirafugratinib versus futibatinib
sec.p: To compare the spectrum of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations emerging at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib and futibatinib in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients, we interrogated the data recently published by Goyal and colleagues (24). Among the cohort of 226 patients with futibatinib and included in their study, we focused on the specific population of FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients FGFR2-driven cholangiocarcinoma experiencing clinical benefit (“i.e. those with an objective response or PFS ≥6 months,” n = 21) assimilable to our definition of acquired resistance. The quantification of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance to futibatinib in this setting was obtained through the data presented in Table 3, Fig. 4, and Supplementary Fig. S3F of ref. 24.

Differences in mutation spectra between inhibitors were assessed using a global exact test based on permutation of inhibitor labels across mutation categories. Statistic applied: χ2 (without correction).

sec.title: Site-directed mutagenesis
sec.p: Lentiviral vectors expressing FGFR2:BICC1 fusions were created using the pLenti6/V5 Directional TOPO Cloning Kit (#K495510, Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Point mutations in the FGFR2 kinase domain of the FGFR2::BICC1 fusion transgene were introduced using the QuikChange XL Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit (#200516, Agilent) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: Ba/F3 cells were infected with lentiviral constructs to express the FGFR2::BICC1 fusion, with or without FGFR2 kinase domain mutations. Ba/F3 cells harboring the fusion were selected in the presence of blasticidin (14 mg/mL) and IL3 (0.5 ng/mL) until recovery and a second selection by culturing the cells in the absence of IL3. FGFR2 fusion and FGFR2 kinase domain mutations were confirmed on the established cell lines by Sanger sequencing. The cells were not tested for Mycoplasma contamination, but cells were not maintained in culture for more than 1 month after establishment or thawing.

sec.title: Viability assays
sec.p: Lirafugratinib and futibatinib were purchased from Selleck Chemicals. Cell viability assays were performed in 96-well plates using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (G7570, Promega). Cells were seeded at a density of 4,000 cells/well and treated for 48 hours. Half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values were derived using GraphPad Prism software (RRID: SCR_002798). For some mutants, the IC50 values reported here have been generated with experiments whose data have been published in our previous work as absolute nM/L values (13). For the purpose of the current paper, we report here the fold change in IC50 value between mutants and wild-type (WT) FGFR2::BICC1.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Ba/F3 cells were treated for 8 hours with 50 nmol/L of either lirafugratinib or futibatinib in the presence of fibroblast growth factor 7 100 ng/mL (R&D Systems, cat. #251-KG), as previously reported (25). The following antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology: pFGFR (RRID: CTS_3471S), pFRS2 (RRID: CTS_3864S), pERK (RRID: CTS_9101S), ERK (RRID: CTS_9102S), pS6 (RRID: CTS_4858S), S6 (RRID: CTS_2217S), and actin (RRID: CTS_3700S). Anti-FGFR2 (RRID: ab10648) and anti-FRS2 (RRID: sc-17841) antibodies were purchased from Abcam and Santa Cruz Biotechnology, respectively.

sec.title: Development of PDX and in vivo pharmacologic studies
sec.p: When possible, post-progression tumor tissue biopsies were used to generate PDXs. Fresh tumor fragments were implanted in the subrenal capsule of six-week-old female NOD/SCID gamma (NSG) mice obtained from Charles River Laboratories (RRID: IMSR_JAX:005557). PDX-bearing NSG mice were treated with the indicated doses of lirafugratinib and futibatinib. Six mice per group were treated for up to 37 days, and tumor volume and mouse weight were measured twice weekly.

All animal procedures and studies have been approved by the French Ministry of “Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l′Innovation” (APAFIS#2790-2015112015055793 and APAFIS#2328-2015101914074846).

sec.title: Structural analyses
sec.p: FGFR2 kinase domain structures from the Protein Data Bank were superimposed based on their C-lobe (residues 660–765) using PyMOL (Schrödinger, RRID: SCR_000305). The angle of C-helix rotation was measured using the Cα atoms of FGFR2 Gly542 and Asp527. The mutations M538I and L618F were generated on the lirafugratinib- or futibatinib-bound FGFR2 structures (PDB ID: 8STG and 8W2X, respectively) using Maestro (Schrödinger).

sec.title: Description of the cohort
sec.p: Between November 2021 and December 2023, 30 patients with FGFR2-driven, advanced solid tumors received lirafugratinib at the RP2D of 70 mg daily in the setting of the ReFocus trial at our institution and could be assessed for resistance mechanisms (Fig. 1). Molecular analyses included targeted NGS on ctDNA and optional WES/bulk RNA-seq on tissue biopsies, performed in the setting of the institutional UNLOCK program running at Gustave Roussy (cohort UNLOCK-03). Eighteen patients suffered from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and 12 from six other tumor types. Nineteen of the tumors were driven by FGFR2 fusions, seven by FGFR2 extracellular domain mutations, two by FGFR2 kinase domain mutations, and one each by FGFR2 truncation and amplification. Eight patients had previously received an FGFR inhibitor, and 22 were FGFR inhibitor–naïve.

caption.p: Presentation of the cohort. A, Samples availability, treatment setting, tumor types, and resistance patterns. B, Baseline characteristics of patients included in the study. #Patient ST4785 was candidate to lirafugratinib due to the detection in ctDNA of FGFR2 N550K and K660M kinase domain mutations. In the progression ctDNA sample, obtained at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, the FGFR2::ATE1 fusion was detected together with the mentioned FGFR2 kinase domain mutations and several others. We cannot exclude that the real driver in this case was the FGFR2 fusion, undetected at baseline and found at progression given the higher tumor fraction in ctDNA. iCCA, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.

sec.p: Considering diverse clinical settings and anticipated resistance patterns, we assessed resistance to lirafugratinib separately in (i) patients previously treated with another FGFR inhibitor; (ii) FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients experiencing primary resistance; and (iii) FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients experiencing acquired resistance.

sec.title: GSEA of tissue biopsies from FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients
sec.p: Leveraging the bulk RNA-seq data obtained from tissue biopsies of FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients, we interrogated whether different expression profiles characterized specific resistance patterns. When comparing GSEA of samples from patients with primary versus acquired resistance, we observed four and 17 hallmarks enriched in the first and second categories, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S1A). Focusing on patients with acquired resistance, 8 and 15 hallmarks were found enriched in cases with FGFR2 kinase domain mutations and with off-target alterations only, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S1B). Given the limited number of patients in each category, these results are to be taken cautiously.

sec.title: Primary and acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in patients pretreated with an FGFR inhibitor
sec.p: Six patients with FGFR2-driven intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and two patients with other tumor types (duodenal cancer and triple-negative breast cancer) were treated with lirafugratinib after progressing on a reversible FGFR inhibitor (n = 6) or futibatinib (n = 2; Fig. 2A; Supplementary Table S1). Patients experienced various degrees of disease response and durations of tumor control, regardless of resistance mechanisms to the previous inhibitors. At progression to lirafugratinib, FGFR2 polyclonal resistance mutations were detected in one patient (ST4131, FGFR2 E566A, and K660M), whereas FGFR2 K660M and V565I were acquired as single mutations in two additional cases (ST3962 and ST238, respectively). Multiple HRAS and KRAS mutations emerged in two patients, co-occurring with FGFR2 kinase domain mutations. As previously reported, patient ST3470 experienced primary disease progression despite the clearance of three FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in ctDNA (13). For patient ST4037, the availability of ctDNA at an early time point after lirafugratinib allowed to evidence the clearance of FGFR2 E566A, L618V, and N550K, the latter reappearing at progression 4 months later (Fig. 2B).

caption.p: Clinical and molecular evolution of patients pretreated with an FGFR inhibitor before undergoing lirafugratinib. A, Overview of the eight patients. Patient ST3962 was the only one to receive intervening chemotherapy between the two FGFR inhibitors and had PD as best response. In this case, the ctDNA at resistance to the first FGFR inhibitor was assessed at progression to chemotherapy. B, Radiologic and molecular (ctDNA) course of patient ST4037 during lirafugratinib treatment. The ctDNA findings are reported as VAF (%). iCCA, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; PD, progressive disease; TBNC, triple-negative breast cancer.

sec.title: Primary resistance to lirafugratinib in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients
sec.p: Six FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients experienced primary resistance to lirafugratinib. In five of these six cases, we detected preexisting molecular alterations potentially limiting the activity of the FGFR2 inhibitor.

The baseline presence of NF1/PTEN mutations, KRAS G12D, high-level FGFR2 amplification (265 copies in ctDNA) could have contributed to the primary resistance in three cases with noncholangiocarcinoma histology (Supplementary Fig. S2). Moreover, patient ST7037 (FGFR2::TACC2 lung adenocarcinoma) had a preexisting NF2 mutation, maintained at progression with the emergence of FGFR2 R451C, occurring on a residue just before the FGFR2 kinase domain.

The remaining two patients suffered from cholangiocarcinoma harboring a FGFR2 mutation. Of note, patient ST6675 had two mutations in the extracellular domain of FGFR2, FGFR2 F276C and Q285K, which we confirmed occurring on the same allele (in cis). Although FGFR2 F276C is a known activating FGFR2 mutation, we cannot exclude that the additional presence of Q285K could modify downstream FGFR2 activation and sensitivity to FGFR inhibition.

sec.title: Acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients
sec.p: Among the 16 patients experiencing acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, 12 (75%) had novel FGFR2 kinase domain mutations detected in samples collected at progression (Fig. 3A). Of major interest, we observed an enrichment of mutations occurring in FGFR2 M538 and L618 residues, namely M538I and L618F. Multiple single-nucleotide variants leading to FGFR2 M538I and FGFR2 L618F were found in 3 of 10 and 6 of 10 of patients acquiring the two mutations, respectively (Supplementary Table S2). In seven patients, FGFR2 M538 and L618 were the only mutated residues, and in four cases, they emerged with other FGFR2 kinase domain mutations. FGFR2 N550K and FGFR2 V565I were detected in two cases, and other FGFR2 kinase domain mutations were found only once across patients, almost invariably at low VAF (Supplementary Table S2). Among these, to the best of our knowledge FGFR2 G584R, L611V, K660S/T, and G664E have not been reported before.

caption.p: Acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients. A, Overview of the alterations found in post-progression samples across 12 patients with on-target resistance. For patients ST3409 and ST4785, NRAS Q61H and BRAF V600E were detected in post-progression ctDNA, respectively. B, Overview of the alterations found in post-progression samples for the three patients with off-target resistance only. C, Distribution of resistance mechanism across the 16 patients experiencing acquired resistance to lirafugratinib. Asterisks indicate the presence of multiple single-nucleotide variants leading to the amino acid change (**, two variants; ***, three variants). In the tissue biopsies of patients ST3409 and ST6059, only one single-nucleotide variant resulting, respectively, in FGFR2 L618F and M538I mutations was found. CUP, cancer of unknown primary; iCCA: intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; mo, months; PDAC, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; PR, partial response.

sec.p: We were able to assess the allelic status of multiple FGFR2 tyrosine kinase mutations detected in the same liquid biopsy sample, when covered by the same sequencing read. In patients ST4193 and ST4785, we confirmed that FGFR2 M538I and N550D/K mutations occurred on different alleles. Patient ST6059 had total of 10 FGFR2 single-nucleotide variants in ctDNA, among which FGFR2 L611V and L618F were on difference alleles, similarly to FGFR2 M538I and N550K detected by tissue biopsy NGS. Single FGFR2 kinase domain mutations were found in the tissue biopsies of additional five patients. These observations reinforce the concept that the polyclonality of resistance arises from mutations in distinct cells, reducing the likelihood of multiple mutations occurring in cis on the same allele.
Multiple ctDNA time points during lirafugratinib treatment were available for two patients, whose clinical and molecular evolution is reported in Supplementary Figs. S3 and S4.

In three cases lacking FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, multiple off-target alterations were found, with an enrichment in KRAS mutations in two of the patients (Fig. 3B; Supplementary Table S3). In one notable case (ST7422), FGFR3::TACC3 was found both in ctDNA and RNA-seq on tissue biopsy.

Taken together, M538 and/or L618 mutations were present in 11 of 16 patients with acquired resistance to lirafugratinib (69%), with additional FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in four of these cases and one (ST3409) with the off-target mutation NRAS Q61H (Fig. 3C; Supplementary Table S2). One patient (ST4785) presented multiple on-target mutations together with the off-target mutation BRAF V600E.

sec.title: Lirafugratinib and futibatinib have complementary activity against FGFR2 kinase domain mutations
sec.p: Among the 16 FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients experiencing acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, we detected a total of 45 single-nucleotide variants resulting in FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (Fig. 3A). To compare the mutational features of acquired resistance to lirafugratinib and futibatinib, we interrogated data from the recent study by Goyal and colleagues (24). In this latter, 21 FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients with FGFR2-driven cholangiocarcinoma underwent post-progression ctDNA analysis after clinical benefit to futibatinib. FGFR2 kinase domain mutations were detected in 18 of 21 (86%) of these patients for a total of 65 single-nucleotide variants leading to FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (data derived from Table 3, Fig. 4, and Supplementary Fig. S3F of ref. 24).

The spectrum of resistance mutations detected after lirafugratinib was significantly different from that observed after futibatinib (exact permutation test on variant-level mutation categories, P < 1 × 10−5). In the present study, 15 FGFR2 M538I and 16 L618F variants and two M538V and L618M mutations were detected at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib [Fig. 4A (left)]. On the other hand, FGFR2 residues M538 and L618, known mutational hotspots to reversible FGFR inhibitors (9, 13), were never found mutated at progression to futibatinib [Fig. 4A (right)]. The molecular brake FGFR2 N550K, which emerged in three patients with acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, is a vulnerability of futibatinib with 15 variants cases detected in the study from Goyal and colleagues (24).

caption.p: Spectrum of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib compared with futibatinib and complementary activity of the two inhibitors. A, Number of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (accounted as single-nucleotide variants) detected in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in the present study (left) and to futibatinib according to Goyal and colleagues (right; ref. 24). B, Variations in IC50 (expressed as fold change compared with WT FGFR2::BICC1) caused by FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in Ba/F3 cellular models. C,In vivo evaluation of lirafugratinib and futibatinib in ST2726 and ST3227 PDXs. D, Number of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (accounted as single-nucleotide variants) detected in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients at acquired resistance to futibatinib according to Goyal and colleagues (left; ref. 24) and lirafugratinib in the present study (right). E, Variations in IC50 (expressed as fold change compared with WT FGFR2::BICC1) caused by FGFR2 kinase domain mutations in Ba/F3 cellular models. iCCA, intrahepatic adenocarcinoma; PDAC, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

sec.p: We then modeled the FGFR2 kinase domain mutations detected at lirafugratinib resistance in Ba/F3 cellular models and evaluated the activity of the two irreversible FGFR inhibitors (Fig. 4B). By measuring the fold change in IC50 value between mutant and WT FGFR2 on a background of FGFR2::BICC1 fusion, we confirmed that M538I and L618F conferred high degree of resistance to lirafugratinib (IC50 fold change >30 and >250, respectively). The two mutations had minimal effect on futibatinib sensitivity (IC50 fold change 3.4 and 2.8, respectively). We observed a low degree of resistance to lirafugratinib in the presence of FGFR2 N550K, V565I, and L618M (ratio IC50 4.3–6.2). Futibatinib retained activity against FGFR2 V565I and L618M, whereas its inefficacy against FGFR2 N550K was confirmed by a ratio IC50 > 25.

Given their clinical relevance at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib, we further interrogated the impact of lirafugratinib and futibatinib on the intracellular signaling in the presence of the FGFR2 M538I or L618F mutations. Both agents inhibited the phosphorylation of the WT FGFR2::BICC1 and of downstream effectors. In the presence of FGFR2 M538I and L618F mutants, only futibatinib significantly reduced the phosphorylation of FGFR2::BICC1, FRS2, ERK1/2, and S6, whereas lirafugratinib had minimal to no effect (Supplementary Fig. S5).

We then established three relevant PDXs of FGFR2-driven tumors directly from patients progressing on lirafugratinib and acquired FGFR2 kinase domain mutations detected on tissue biopsies and confirmed in the animal models: ST2726 with FGFR2 M538I, ST3227 with FGFR2 L618F (Fig. 4C), and ST4193 with FGFR2 V565I (Supplementary Fig. S6). In these PDXs, although lirafugratinib had no activity, futibatinib abrogated (ST2726, ST3227) or significantly reduced (ST4193) tumor growth, confirming the activity of futibatinib at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in vivo.

These molecular and functional correlations suggested a potential treatment sequence of lirafugratinib followed by futibatinib, as resistance mutations can be overcome. Envisioning a potential inverse treatment sequence, we performed the same analysis as in Fig. 4A, moving from the mutations observed at acquired resistance to futibatinib (Fig. 4D). FGFR2 N550D/H/K and V565F/L mutations were markers of futibatinib resistance, whereas only four FGFR2 N550K single-nucleotide variants (in three patients) and two V565I mutations emerged at lirafugratinib resistance. Here too, the clinical observations matched with the IC50 data (Fig. 4E), endorsing the potential of sequential treatment with futibatinib followed by lirafugratinib, a strategy already confirmed in three PDX models harboring molecular brake or gatekeeper FGFR2 mutations in our previous work (13).

sec.title: Structural analysis of FGFR2 inhibitor binding and resistance mutations
sec.p: To understand how resistance mutations differentially affect the sensitivity of FGFR2 to lirafugratinib and futibatinib, we conducted a structural analysis of FGFR2 using available FGFR2 kinase domain structures. The activation of FGFR kinase involves conformational closure through N-lobe rotation toward the C-lobe, forming an active conformation (26, 27). Structural superposition of FGFR2 harboring activating or gain-of-function mutations showed that they adopt a closed conformation similar to that of phosphorylated, active FGFR2 (Fig. 5A). The resistance mutations M538I and L618F have previously been characterized to promote this active conformation by altering local interaction networks within the αC tether and DFG latch regions, respectively (28).

caption.p: Structural analysis of FGFR2 with FGFR2 M538I and L618F mutations. A, Superposition of FGFR2 kinase domain structures bearing activating mutations or gain-of-function mutations (colored in white) with FGFR kinase domain structures containing lirafugratinib (colored in green) and futibatinib (colored in salmon). Superimposed structures are from the Protein Data Bank entries 2pvf (phosphorylated, active WT), 2pvy, 2pwl, 2py3, 2pz5, 2pzp, 2pzr, 2q0b, 4j95, 4j96, 4j97, 4j98, 4j99, 5ugl, 5ugx, 5uhn, 5ui0, 8stg (lirafugratinib), and 8w2x (futibatinib). B, Close-up views of the ATP-binding pocket and αC-helix region. Structures of the FGFR2 kinase domain in complex with lirafugratinib or futibatinib are shown in green and salmon, respectively. Key residues involved in inhibitor binding are depicted as sticks. Resistance mutations M538I and L618F are modeled using Maestro (Schrödinger) and shown as sticks in white.

sec.p: Structural superposition of FGFR2 in complex with either lirafugratinib or futibatinib reveals that both inhibitors bind to FGFR2 in an open, inactive-like conformation (Fig. 5A). Notably, lirafugratinib stabilizes a more pronounced open conformation compared with futibatinib (Fig. 5A). This structural difference may underlie the reduced tolerance of lirafugratinib to resistance mutations such as M538I and L618F, which promote an active-like conformation. Local interaction analysis further reveals that lirafugratinib forms a van der Waals contact with M538 and participates in a hydrophobic interaction network involving L618 and F646 residues (Fig. 5B). The M538I mutation eliminates such van der Waals contact, although the substitution of leucine with the bulkier phenylalanine in L618 (L618F) perturbs the hydrophobic network, both likely diminishing lirafugratinib binding (Fig. 5B). In contrast, futibatinib binds less deeply into the pocket and engages minimally with these residues, rendering it less sensitive to such mutations.

sec.title: Clinical activity of treatment sequences with lirafugratinib and futibatinib
sec.p: The mutational landscape of FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib and futibatinib, respectively, corroborated by the in vitro/in vivo proof of the complementarity of the two irreversible inhibitors, prompted the proposal of sequential treatment strategies (Fig. 6A).

caption.p: Proposal and clinical activity of treatment sequences with lirafugratinib and futibatinib. A, Proposal of therapeutic strategies with the sequential use of irreversible FGFR inhibitors based on FGFR2 kinase domain mutations emerging at acquired resistance. B, Clinical and molecular evolution of patient ST3536. C, Clinical and molecular evolution of patient ST3227. D, Clinical and molecular evolution of patient MR822. The ctDNA findings are reported as VAF (%). CUP, cancer of unknown primary; iCCA, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; PD, progressive disease; PDAC, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; PR, partial response.

sec.p: Although FGFR2 mutations in M538 and L618 position are not the only ones detected at progression to lirafugratinib, their dominance dictates the sequential strategy proposed, similarly for FGFR2 mutations in the molecular brake (N550) and gatekeeper (V565) residues causing resistance to futibatinib. It should be noted that we cannot definitely claim the activity of lirafugratinib against FGFR2 N550K mutation, given it emerged, still rarely, in the post-lirafugratinib setting, and the borderline IC50 values.

We previously reported the clinical validation of lirafugratinib activity in patients with acquired resistance to futibatinib (13). Here, we report the prolonged clinical benefit in patients receiving lirafugratinib followed by futibatinib. Futibatinib’s recent approval and commercial availability in Europe restricted the lirafugratinib–futibatinib sequence to two patients of this cohort.

Patient ST3536 had a FGFR2::MITF–driven cancer of unknown primary, who benefitted from lirafugratinib for more than 1 year (Fig. 6B). At progression, ctDNA showed FGFR2::MITF fusion and FGFR2 M538I/V and L618F mutations. After an interval period of 1 year and 8 months, during which chemotherapy was administered, the patient developed ascites requiring weekly paracentesis. At this time point, ctDNA found the known FGFR2 fusion and FGFR2 M538I/V and L611P mutations. Futibatinib was started, and clinical benefit was evident with no longer need for paracentesis. At 3 months since futibatinib start, all FGFR2 alterations were cleared in the ctDNA with the exception of FGFR2 M538I, persisting at reduced VAF.

Patient ST3227 suffered from a FGFR2-rearranged pancreatic adenocarcinoma, treated with lirafugratinib as the third treatment line. Longitudinal ctDNA showed the clearance of the driver FGFR2 fusion, with the progressive increase in the VAF of FGFR2 L618F mutation, also detected in the tissue biopsy obtained at lirafugratinib progression (Fig. 6C). The patient received chemotherapy and was then candidate to futibatinib treatment, with an interval of 1 year and 4 months between the two inhibitors. The ctDNA analysis before futibatinib confirmed the persistence of FGFR2 L618F mutation, and the irreversible inhibitor led to regression of the hepatic lesions.

Patient MR822 (FGFR2-rearranged intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma) achieved prolonged clinical benefit with pemigatinib and lirafugratinib, with FGFR2 N550T emerging after the reversible inhibitor and no ctDNA shedding at progression to the irreversible inhibitor (see Fig. 2A). Following intervening chemotherapy, the patient received futibatinib with a marked and prolonged disease response, ongoing after a year (Fig. 6D).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: FGFR inhibition represents a novel paradigm in precision oncology, from cholangiocarcinoma to other tumors driven by FGFR2 alterations. The identification of recurrent patterns of resistance to FGFR inhibitors is a key to envision treatment strategies, with the sequential use of targeted agents. In this work, we identified molecular liabilities at acquired resistance to lirafugratinib that can be overcome by futibatinib, supporting the adoption of sequential treatments with irreversible FGFR inhibitors in clinical practice.

Our initial observation was stemmed from molecular and clinical evolution of patients receiving lirafugratinib after progressing on a previous FGFR inhibitor. We encountered difficulties in delineating treatment strategies, including reversible inhibitors followed by irreversible ones, as we have already shown for futibatinib (13). Primary resistance to lirafugratinib can occur despite its ability to target FGFR2 kinase domain mutations emerging after reversible inhibitors. We suppose that the high heterogeneity at resistance to reversible FGFR inhibitors goes beyond already documented FGFR2 kinase domain mutations (9, 13), including additional nongenetic undetectable mechanisms that hamper lirafugratinib activity. Another point of interest is that even after experiencing clinical benefit from the selective FGFR2 inhibitor, patients do not develop FGFR2 M538 and L618 mutations, in contrast with what we observed in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients treated with lirafugratinib.

The findings on primary resistance to lirafugratinib in FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients are of potential clinical interest. A larger, systematic work on patients encountering de novo resistance would be required to provide clinical recommendations. Nevertheless, we propose that baseline alterations known to drive off-target resistance to targeted agents, as well as very high levels of FGFR2 amplification or previously unreported FGFR2 mutations in the extracellular domain, could generate a lack of activity of FGFR inhibitors. These baseline co-alterations should therefore be taken into account in patient selection.

Among 16 FGFR inhibitor–naïve patients, we were able to identify molecular alterations potentially causing acquired resistance to lirafugratinib in all but one case (94%). The main finding here was the detection of recurrent FGFR2 kinase domain mutations at acquired resistance mutations to lirafugratinib, namely FGFR2 M538I and L618F. Substitutions occurring at FGFR2 M538 and L618 residues (analogous to FGFR2 M537 and L617 according to another common transcript of reference) have been reported at resistance to reversible FGFR inhibitors and do not emerge at progression to futibatinib (9, 13). Leveraging the recent work from Goyal and colleagues (24) on futibatinib in a setting similar to ours, we revealed a strong complementarity between the two irreversible inhibitors in terms of activity against FGFR2 kinase domain mutations. In line with the preclinical activity of the FGFR2-selective inhibitor (13, 16, 17), our clinical data from patients progressing on lirafugratinib witnessed the rare emergence of FGFR2 molecular brake and gatekeeper mutations, which are more frequent at futibatinib failure (9, 13). On the other hand, FGFR2 M538I and L618F mutations frequently emerged and cause high degree of resistance to lirafugratinib, still maintaining sensitivity to futibatinib in vitro and in vivo. The simultaneous administration of the two inhibitors, to prevent the emergence of any on-target resistance mutation, could likely not be pursued given their toxicity already as single agents, with overlapping adverse events (29). An ideal FGFR2 inhibitor would therefore require selectivity and activity on all the potential FGFR2 kinase domain mutations, still maintaining a reasonable safety profile.

Our structural analyses revealed that the binding of lirafugratinib to FGFR2 relies on precise structural complementarities, which likely underlie both its selectivity and its susceptibility to distinctive activating resistance mutations. These findings highlight the need for careful structure–activity relationship optimization to enhance activity against mutation-driven resistance for the development of novel inhibitors.

Several patients receiving lirafugratinib in the setting of clinical trials in our institution were ideal candidates with sequential treatment with futibatinib. Nevertheless, the latter inhibitor was not commercially available in Europe until recently, and only three patients could receive it after progressing on lirafugratinib and after receiving additional systemic therapies. It should be noted that these patients experienced a prolonged interval between the two inhibitors, suggesting a particularly indolent biology of their disease.

Nevertheless, the story of these three patients achieving disease response to futibatinib after having progressed on lirafugratinib vouches for the clinical utility of the sequence. As this work focuses originally on resistance to lirafugratinib, our proposal for the clinical implementation of a treatment sequence of FGFR inhibitors sees lirafugratinib followed by futibatinib. Nevertheless, the complementarity of the two irreversible inhibitors against FGFR2 kinase domain mutations supports the inverse sequence as well, as shown in our previous work (13).

The present work provides the first preclinical and clinical support to envision such sequences. Academic efforts to collect and report large series of patients treated according to this strategy will therefore be desirable to assess its real clinical impact. Although futibatinib is currently approved for FGFR2-driven cholangiocarcinoma, lirafugratinib approval is awaited between 2026 and 2027, initially with the same indication, and subsequently as a tumor-agnostic treatment (30). Although we report a limited number of cases with a non-cholangiocarcinoma histology, we believe our work vouches for the study of resistance mechanisms in a tumor-agnostic manner, sustaining a sequential utility of the two inhibitors regardless of the tissue of origin. Indeed, among the three patients who received futibatinib after lirafugratinib, two had a non-cholangiocarcinoma tumor.

The main limitation of our study is its exclusive focus on genetic mechanisms of resistance, whereas other features such as lineage plasticity, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and microenvironmental adaptations were not assessed. The relatively small sample size was a limiting factor on evaluating the impact of tumor types, FGFR2 driver alterations, and prior treatments on resistance patterns. Moreover, several cases missed the collection of post-progression tissue for WES/RNA-seq study, which would be of interest in identifying potential resistance mechanisms in cases with lack of ctDNA shedding. Three panels were used to analyze liquid biopsy samples, introducing a source of technical variability. Our in vivo models were established from tissue biopsies containing one FGFR2 kinase domain mutation only, also in cases with multiple alterations documented by ctDNA, modulating therefore the clinical meaning of our pharmacologic studies. Although PDXs cannot recapitulate the global heterogeneity of patients’ tumors at resistance, they still represent a highly valuable model to test inhibitors activity. Finally, although we provide initial evidence supporting the validity of FGFR inhibitor sequences, robust clinical evidence is lacking, mainly in terms of direct switches between inhibitors without intervening therapies.

In conclusion, the field of FGFR2 inhibition in cholangiocarcinoma and other FGFR2-driven tumors is in continuous evolution given the clinical development of novel agents (31–34). Although awaiting clinical data on these inhibitors, we analyzed resistance patterns to lirafugratinib and identified recurrent resistance mutations that remain sensitive to futibatinib treatment. The two irreversible inhibitors are the most promising agents thus far available in this setting, and in the presence of precise FGFR2 resistance mutations, they can be used sequentially in patients with FGFR2-driven tumors.
